result.question: Best practices for CODING AGENTS' repo context and code-quality enforcement (2025-2026), to inform building a shippable pi-framework agent harness (nana-pi). Two sub-lanes: (1) How coding agents should navigate and understand repos: CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md conventions including NESTED per-folder AGENTS.md files, llms.txt, aider-style tree-sitter repo maps, generated architecture maps/indexes; what leading tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Aider, OpenAI Codex CLI, Copilot, Amp, opencode) actually do; any evidence or practitioner consensus on which navigation/context conventions actually improve agent output vs. add noise; context-rot/token-cost tradeoffs of large context files. (2) Enforcing modularity and quality on AGENT-GENERATED code: deterministic gates wired into the agent loop (lint/format/type-check hooks on every edit, test gates, file-length caps like ESLint max-lines / max-lines-per-function, complexity caps like ruff C901 / radon / xenon; pre-commit); documented failure modes of agent-generated code (file bloat, duplication, dead code, over-nesting) and which countermeasures practitioners report actually work (hard caps + auto-reject vs. prompt guidance vs. review passes).
result.summary: For repo navigation and context: the strongest, most-replicated finding is that lean, high-signal context files beat exhaustive ones. Context rot is measured across 18 frontier models (performance degrades as input grows, worsens with low query-relevance, and position/presentation matters more than mere presence), and agent instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) specifically bloat over time, conflict, and lose rule adherence as they grow — so split nested per-directory files past ~150-200 lines with closest-file-wins precedence. Leading agents (Claude Code) favor just-in-time grep/glob retrieval with only small context files plus lightweight identifiers pre-loaded, rather than large pre-computed indexes; structural indexes (aider repo maps, tree-sitter knowledge graphs, SCIP/LSP) cut token cost ~10x and give precise exact navigation but trade general-comprehension quality (83% vs 92%) and rest largely on a single unreplicated study. For quality enforcement on agent-generated code, the well-documented pattern is deterministic gates wired into the agent loop — a PreToolUse hard-block and a PostToolUse checker-on-every-edit, with exit-code-2 un-bypassable even by an allow decision — motivated by a measured procedural-bloat failure mode in LLM code. Critically, the two claims that would most directly justify prompt-only mitigation being useless and hard file-length caps (a rho=0.94 volume→decay correlation) both FAILED verification, so the case for deterministic gates rests on mechanism plus practitioner consensus, not on those comparative measurements.

findings.claim: Context rot is real and measured: LLM performance degrades as input token count grows even on simple retrieval, across all 18 frontier models tested (GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, Qwen3); degradation is worse when target info is low-similarity to the query, and how info is presented/positioned matters more than its mere presence. Models have a finite attention budget depleted by every token, so good context engineering targets the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens, not maximal context.
findings.vote: unanimous 3-0 across claims 4,5,6,10; 2-1 on claim 9 (CLAUDE.md-specific 'direct evidence' framing slightly overstated)
findings.evidence: Chroma Context Rot report (primary, July 2025) tested exactly 18 models and states verbatim performance 'grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows,' 'degrades more quickly... with lower similarity needle-question pairs,' and 'what matters more is how that information is presented.' Independently replicated by Liu et al. Lost-in-the-Middle (TACL, peer-reviewed), Adobe NoLiMa, Veseli/Du 2025. Anthropic's context-engineering guidance (primary) supplies the attention-budget mechanism ('Every new token introduced depletes this budget') and the 'smallest possible set of high-signal tokens' principle. Caveat: context-rot evidence is for long context in general and applies to CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md files by sound inference, not by direct measurement of instruction files; Chroma sells vector-DB tooling (mild commercial incentive) but the effect replicates independently.

findings.claim: Agent instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) accumulate over time as teams add overviews/architecture/conventions/rules, grow long enough that instructions conflict ('agent instruction bloat'), and as they grow the probability that important rules get ignored increases — bigger context files degrade rule adherence rather than improve it. A lost-in-the-middle effect applies specifically: guidance buried deep in a long instruction file is more likely to be missed.
findings.vote: unanimous 3-0 across claims 18,19,20; secondary source with strong academic corroboration
findings.evidence: Thoughtworks Technology Radar Vol.34 (Apr 2026, status Hold) names the anti-pattern verbatim and states 'As instructions grow, the likelihood increases that important rules are ignored' and 'Models tend to attend less to content buried in the middle of long contexts.' Corroborated by an ETH Zurich finding that AGENTS.md context files reduced task success while inflating inference cost ~20%, and by a converging practitioner-cited ~150-200 discrete-instruction adherence ceiling (Augment 'junk drawer', HumanLayer, Arize). One refinement, not a contradiction: an instruction-following study found the positional lost-in-the-middle mechanism did not drive the degradation — the driver is discrete-instruction count/bloat rather than raw byte position — but adherence still fell as instruction count rose. No source found claiming larger/more-detailed files improve adherence.

findings.claim: Leading coding agents favor just-in-time retrieval over pre-loaded indexes: Claude Code uses a hybrid model where small CLAUDE.md files are dropped into context up front while glob/grep primitives navigate the repo and retrieve files just-in-time, keeping only lightweight identifiers (file paths, stored queries, links) in context and loading data dynamically via tools — bypassing stale indexing and complex syntax trees. This is an argument against large pre-loaded context/index files, but the recommended shape is a hybrid, not pure JIT.
findings.vote: 3-0 on claim 7; 2-1 on claim 8 (interpretive tail 'argument against large index files' — the article itself recommends a hybrid)
findings.evidence: Anthropic engineering blog (primary) states Claude Code 'employs this hybrid model: CLAUDE.md files are naively dropped into context up front, while primitives like glob and grep allow it to navigate its environment and retrieve files just-in-time, effectively bypassing the issues of stale indexing and complex syntax trees,' and defines JIT as maintaining 'lightweight identifiers... and use these references to dynamically load data into context at runtime.' Corroborated by Anthropic's May-2025 removal of vector search from Claude Code (grep 'outperformed everything. By a lot.' — Boris Cherny) and third-party writeups (Vadim 'Claude Code Doesn't Index Your Codebase'). Important guard: the same article warns pure runtime exploration 'is slower than retrieving pre-computed data' and keeps a small pre-loaded file — do not stretch this into 'never pre-load anything'; the target is LARGE pre-computed indexes.

findings.claim: A repo map is a deliberately token-minimal structural index (file + symbol listing) that exists specifically to avoid sending whole files, which wastes the limited context window; with the map in context the agent can autonomously decide which files it needs to open and request them (with user approval), instead of the user manually selecting the relevant file set.
findings.vote: 3-0 on claim 0; 2-1 on claim 1 (the cited ctags page is deprecated; 'autonomously open' glosses the ask-then-approve step)
findings.evidence: Aider docs (primary, tool author's own design docs): 'Sending whole files is a bulky way to send code context, wasting the precious 8k context window,' and 'If it needs to see more code, [the model] can use the map to figure out by itself which files it needs to look at... aider will automatically add them to the chat context (with user approval).' The cited ctags.html is historical (8k-era) but the current repomap.html carries the principle forward: 'concise map of your whole git repository' with a dynamic token budget (--map-tokens, default 1k). Note: the related claim that the map includes callable SIGNATURES was REFUTED (0-3) — treat the map as a file+symbol listing, not signature-level.

findings.claim: Structural code indexes (tree-sitter knowledge graphs via MCP, SCIP/LSP semantic graphs) materially reduce agent context cost — ~10x fewer tokens and ~2.1x fewer tool calls across 31 repos vs a file-exploration agent — and are more precise than text search or embeddings for exact navigation (go-to-definition, find-references, impact analysis). But this is a tradeoff, not a free win: the graph agent reached only 83% answer quality vs 92% for file exploration on general queries (matching/exceeding it only on graph-native structural queries in 19/31 languages), and the 10x token result is a single unreplicated vendor self-benchmark. Embeddings surface related intent but do not capture the symbol relationships refactoring needs.
findings.vote: unanimous 3-0 across claims 2,3,16,17; but a single-study primary (self-benchmark) plus secondary sweep
findings.evidence: arXiv:2603.27277 (Vogel et al., Mar 2026, primary) reports '83% answer quality versus 92% for a file-exploration agent, at ten times fewer tokens and 2.1 times fewer tool calls' across 31 real-world repos, matching or exceeding the explorer on graph-native queries in 19/31 languages; a secondary sweep (anthonywest.co.uk) quotes these verbatim and explicitly flags them as 'one system, one evaluation design and one paper... directional rather than settled.' SCIP precision is backed by Sourcegraph's own docs (SCIP navigation is 'compiler-accurate' vs search-based 'false-positive and false-negative results'). Caveats: the arXiv figures are a single-author vendor self-benchmark with n=1 human judge grading against his own reference answers, unreplicated; the 83%<92% quality drop runs against author interest (so trustworthy) — do NOT cite structural indexing as strictly better. Whether the extra precision is worth the cost for LLM agents is a live, unsettled practitioner debate (Claude Code leans grep; Cursor uses a hybrid).

findings.claim: AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md should start as a single file and split into nested per-directory files once it exceeds ~150-200 lines; agents read the file closest to the file being edited and, on conflicting instructions, more deeply nested files take precedence.
findings.vote: 3-0 on claim 21; precedence is spec-backed, the line threshold is a practitioner heuristic only
findings.evidence: The official agents.md spec confirms the precedence mechanism verbatim: 'Agents automatically read the nearest file in the directory tree, so the closest one takes precedence,' with explicit monorepo/subproject support. The '150-200 line' split threshold is NOT in the spec — it is a soft heuristic echoed across multiple independent practitioner sources (Augment guide, 0xfauzi best-practices gist) and contradicted nowhere. Caveat lowering confidence: implementations diverge on merge-vs-override — OpenAI Codex CONCATENATES all AGENTS.md from root to cwd, and Cursor layers parents with more-specific-wins, rather than reading only the closest file. 'Deeper wins on conflict' survives all implementations, but the merge behavior is not uniform.

findings.claim: Deterministic quality gates can be wired directly into the agent loop rather than left to prompt guidance: hooks fire on every tool call (PreToolUse / PostToolUse). A PreToolUse hook can hard-block a tool call before it executes (e.g. deny destructive shell commands), giving a deterministic auto-reject gate in front of edits/commands. A PostToolUse hook matched to Edit|Write runs a linter/formatter/security-scan automatically after each edit (the checker-on-every-edit pattern). Exit code 2 is an un-bypassable block whose stderr/reason is fed back to the model — it holds even against a JSON permissionDecision of 'allow', so the gate cannot be loosened by the model's own decision output.
findings.vote: unanimous 3-0 across claims 11,12,13,14; all primary official docs
findings.evidence: Claude Code hooks docs (primary): hooks fire 'on every tool call inside the agentic loop: PreToolUse and PostToolUse'; PreToolUse 'Blocks the tool call' with a worked rm-rf deny example; the exact PostToolUse '{matcher: Edit|Write, command: lint-check.sh}' example runs a linter only on writes/edits; and 'Exit 2 means a blocking error... even a JSON permissionDecision of allow can't override it.' Independent practitioners (morphllm, hidekazu-konishi, blakecrosley) corroborate hooks as 'the deterministic shell around the probabilistic agent' — 'runs the linter every time, because the harness runs it, not Claude.' Note the asymmetry: PostToolUse runs AFTER the tool succeeds so it gives feedback rather than a hard pre-write reject; a true auto-reject-before-write requires PreToolUse. These are Claude-Code-specific APIs — the mechanism transfers to pi's hook classes but the exact API does not.

findings.claim: Agent/LLM-generated code has a measured procedural-bloat failure mode: zero-shot LLM code produces far more Long Method smells than human code (Qwen-coder-480B generated 11 Long Methods vs 1 for the human baseline; 4 of 5 models exceeded the human baseline). This documents file/method bloat as a quantified, real failure mode motivating structural quality controls — but the specific countermeasure ranking (prompts vs caps vs gates) is NOT settled by the evidence.
findings.vote: 2-1 on claim 15 (the 'agent' label is imprecise — 11-vs-1 is zero-shot LLM, not agentic); single study
findings.evidence: arXiv:2605.02741 (Zhu/Tsantalis/Rigby, Concordia, May 2026 — credible authors; Tsantalis wrote RefactoringMiner) Table 1: zero-shot Long Method counts deepseek 2 / Qwen-30b 7 / Qwen-480b 11 / Gemini-2.5-pro 5 vs human 1. IMPORTANT SCOPING: the paper's actual AGENTIC experiment (MetaGPT) shifted toward ARCHITECTURAL smells (God Classes, Too Many Branches), NOT Long Method — so procedural bloat is a zero-shot-LLM signature, architectural bloat is the agent-driven signature. Sample is modest (90 CodeContest problems). Two related claims from the same paper were REFUTED: that prompt engineering fails to reduce smells (p>0.8) went 1-2, and that code volume predicts architectural decay at rho=0.94 went 0-3. So the evidence supports 'agent code bloats' but does NOT support 'prompts are useless' or 'hard file-length caps are high-leverage per a strong volume-decay correlation.'

result.caveats:
SOURCE QUALITY: The context-rot cluster is strongest — primary Anthropic + Chroma sources with peer-reviewed replication (Liu Lost-in-the-Middle, NoLiMa, ETH Zurich). Chroma sells vector-DB tooling (mild incentive to frame long context as unreliable), but the effect replicates independently. The instruction-bloat/nested-AGENTS.md findings rest on secondary practitioner sources (Thoughtworks Radar, Augment) — well-corroborated but not primary experiments. The structural-index 10x/2.1x figures are a SINGLE unreplicated single-author vendor self-benchmark (arXiv 2603.27277, n=1 human judge grading its own reference answers); treat as directional. The hook/gate mechanism claims are maximally solid (official Claude Code docs) but Claude-Code-specific — mechanism transfers to pi, exact API does not.

REFUTED CLAIMS THAT CONSTRAIN THE RECOMMENDATION (do not cite these): (1) 'Prompt guidance is ineffective at reducing code smells (p>0.8)' failed verification (1-2) — you cannot claim prompt-based mitigation is useless. (2) 'Code volume predicts architectural decay at rho=0.94' failed (0-3) — hard file-length caps (ESLint max-lines etc.) do NOT have that strong empirical backing; the volume-decay correlation is not established. (3) 'Aider repo map includes callable signatures' failed (0-3) — the map is a file+symbol listing, not signature-level. Net: the case for deterministic gates rests on documented MECHANISM + practitioner consensus, not on a proven prompts-lose / caps-win comparison.

SCOPING NUANCES: (a) Context-rot evidence is for long context in general; its application to CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md instruction files is sound inference, not direct measurement of such files. (b) The agent-code-bloat number (11 Long Methods) is ZERO-SHOT LLM; the paper's agentic (MetaGPT) experiment showed a shift to ARCHITECTURAL smells (God Class), so procedural-bloat gates and architectural-bloat gates may catch different things. (c) The '150-200 line split' threshold is a practitioner heuristic, NOT in the official AGENTS.md spec, and implementations diverge on merge-vs-override (Codex concatenates root→cwd; Cursor/spec = closest wins). (d) The JIT-vs-index question resolves to a HYBRID in the sources, not pure JIT — small files pre-loaded, large indexes avoided.

TIME-SENSITIVITY: All sources are 2025-2026 and current for a 2026-09 build. The aider ctags page is explicitly deprecated (superseded by tree-sitter repomap). The whole grep-JIT-vs-semantic-index question is an actively contested, moving practitioner debate — expect the consensus to shift as tools iterate.
openQuestions: Does the pi framework's hook system expose the specific semantics nana-pi needs — a PreToolUse hard-block AND an un-bypassable exit-code-2-equivalent that the model cannot loosen? Memory notes all 4 pi hook classes were verified, but the block-before-execute and un-bypassability guarantees should be confirmed against pi's own hook docs, not assumed from the Claude Code contract.

With the rho=0.94 volume→decay claim refuted, what line-count / complexity thresholds (max-lines, C901, radon/xenon) actually reduce agent bloat in practice? No verified empirical threshold survived — the caps may still be worth wiring as deterministic gates on mechanism grounds, but their leverage is unquantified.

Since agentic code generation's dominant smell appears to be architectural (God Class, too-many-branches) rather than procedural (Long Method), which gates catch each class, and does a modularity/complexity cap need to operate at the file/class boundary rather than just per-function?

For a shippable nana-pi harness on real (possibly large) repos, does grep/glob JIT alone suffice (Claude Code's bet) or does adding a tree-sitter repo map / SCIP index measurably improve output — and at what repo size does the ~10x token saving outweigh the ~9-point general-comprehension quality drop? The single-study evidence leaves this unresolved.

refuted.claim: Aider's repo map lists every file in the repo plus the symbols defined in each file, and for callables (functions/methods) it also includes their signatures — giving the model a structural index without the full source.

Prompt engineering does not improve agent code quality: structured few-shot prompting and more detailed/specific requirements produced no statistically significant reduction in code smells (p>0.8), and specifically failed to reduce Long Method smells. This is direct evidence that prompt guidance alone is an ineffective countermeasure — favoring deterministic gates over prompt-based mitigation.

Code volume is a near-perfect predictor of architectural decay: total lines of code correlated with architectural smells at rho=0.94 (p<0.001). This directly supports file-length / volume caps (ESLint max-lines, etc.) as a high-leverage deterministic control on agent output.
